title: Senior's toolkit: statistics in code
summary: The scipy.stats tests analysts run every week, bootstrap intervals, correlation that survives outliers, and sizing an A/B test.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: statistics in code
steps.body: You built the ideas by simulation. At work the same questions are answered with a few well-known calls, and the skill is picking the right one and stating its assumptions.

toolkit.what: Compare the means of two independent groups (for example average order value in A and B).
flags: Welch's t-test: do not assume equal spreads (the safe default to choose)
a one-sided test, decided before you look
toolkit.example:
from scipy import stats
res = stats.ttest_ind(b_values, a_values, equal_var=False)
print(res.pvalue)

toolkit.what: Test whether two categories are related, from a table of counts (for example converted yes/no by variant).
flags: the counts you would expect if they were unrelated

toolkit.what: Compare two groups without assuming normal data. Good for skewed values such as delivery times.
A 95% bootstrap confidence interval: resample with replacement many times, then take the middle 95% of the results.
toolkit.example:
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
boot = [rng.choice(x, size=len(x)).mean() for _ in range(10_000)]
low, high = np.percentile(boot, [2.5, 97.5])

toolkit.what: Shuffle the group labels to see what differences chance alone produces: a permutation test with no distribution assumptions.
Correlation between columns. Spearman uses ranks, so one extreme value cannot drive it, and it catches any steady (monotonic) trend.
How many users each group needs before you start an A/B test (statsmodels). Fix the sample size first; do not stop when it looks significant.
flags: the smallest effect worth detecting, in standard deviations
chance of detecting a real effect
toolkit.example:
from statsmodels.stats.power import TTestIndPower
n = TTestIndPower().solve_power(effect_size=0.2, alpha=0.05, power=0.8)

steps.prompt: A product manager checked the A/B dashboard every morning and stopped the test on day 3, the first day p dropped below 0.05. Why is that result not trustworthy?
options: Peeking: checking many times and stopping at the first p < 0.05 makes a false positive far more likely than 5%. Fix the sample size in advance (a power calculation) and test once
Three days is always too short for any test
The test should have used a 0.01 threshold every day
steps.explain: Each look is another chance for noise to cross the line. The 5% error rate only holds for one test at a planned sample size, unless you use a method designed for sequential looks.

steps.prompt: Which test or measure fits the question?
items: Is average order value different between variant A and B?
Do two apps have different mean session lengths (very different spreads)?
Does conversion (yes/no) depend on the variant?
Is device type related to whether users churn?
Do higher-priced products get lower ratings, with a few extreme prices?
Does delivery time rank go with complaint count?

steps.prompt: Run Welch's t-test on two groups and print the p-value.
steps.explain: `equal_var=False` gives Welch's test, which does not assume both groups have the same variance. The result has `statistic` and `pvalue` fields.

steps.prompt: Delivery times in minutes, one of them a stuck order. What does this print?
steps.explain: One extreme value drags the mean to 42.4 minutes, which describes no real delivery. The median, 14, is what a typical customer saw. Report the median (and look at the outlier) for skewed data.

steps.prompt: Match each argument to what it means.
pairs: 80% chance of detecting a real effect

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Before an experiment, write down the metric, the test and the sample size from a power calculation; afterwards, report an interval, not only a p-value. For skewed data, look at medians, Spearman and rank tests before you trust a mean.
